lesson_title: Chemistry That Pays in Electricity: Galvanic Cells
hook_text: Drop zinc into blue copper solution and the energy burns off as heat. Split the beaker in two... and it powers your phone.
clip_script: Drop a strip of zinc into blue copper solution and chemistry happens instantly: zinc dissolves, brown copper crusts out, the blue fades — and all the energy escapes as useless heat. Money, burned. Now the trick behind every battery on Earth: separate them. Zinc in one beaker, copper solution in the other, so the electrons cannot jump across directly. The only route left runs through YOUR wire — and electrons marching through a wire is an electric current. Same reaction, but now it commutes through your torch, your calculator, your phone. Why does it work? Some substances are electron givers, some are grabbers, and chemistry publishes the league table: standard electrode potentials, every species ranked against hydrogen's zero. Copper outranks zinc, so copper ions grab and zinc gives — and the gap between their rankings IS the voltage: 0,34 minus negative 0,76 — 1,10 volts. Want more? Pair magnesium with silver, opposite ends of the table: 3,16 volts. One warning: the whole enterprise dies without the salt bridge quietly shuttling ions to keep both beakers neutral. Pull it out and the voltage slams to zero. And a flat battery? Nothing leaked — the reaction simply reached equilibrium. Chemistry clocked out.
visual_style: A beaker splitting into two with a wire arcing between them, electrons queuing through a glowing bulb; a league table of elements with copper above zinc and the gap highlighted as volts; a salt bridge shuttling ion traffic below.
mood: Entrepreneurial chemistry — the same reaction, rerouted into profit.
pacing: Wasted-heat hook, split-beaker reveal, league-table beat, salt-bridge warning, equilibrium punchline.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and read the table that predicts every battery's voltage.
